title: Thirty-nine kinds of work
hookLine: Shabbat's labors are drawn from building the tabernacle (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)

cards: Read the list out loud and something odd happens. Sowing. Plowing.

teach.b: Avot melacha. Avot means fathers, so these are the fathers of work, the main categories. The Mishnah opens its list with the total: forty less one.
Back in year one you met the big idea, that the rabbis connect these kinds of work to the building of the tabernacle. Today, the machinery. First, the order.

teach.h: CHAINS OF MAKING: BREAD, CLOTH, SCROLL.
teach.b: The list follows whole chains of making: bread, then cloth, then the hide for writing, then building and tearing down, putting out and kindling a fire, the final hammer blow that finishes a thing, and carrying from one domain to another.

The Talmud asks why baking is on the list when the tabernacle needed dyes cooked, not bread baked, and answers that the Mishnah followed the order of bread. It was built to be remembered, chain by chain.
If there are fathers, there are offspring. The rabbis call them toldot: acts that share the father's purpose without looking like it.
The Talmud's example: pruning a tree counts under planting, because both help a plant grow. So the thirty-nine aren't a fence around thirty-nine actions.
They're thirty-nine questions to ask of any new act: which father does this belong to? Third, why count at all?

The Mishnah's own setting is a case of someone who forgot, and in its rulings, how many fathers you broke matters for what you owe. A definition, not a mood. Shabbat doesn't say rest however you like.
It says here is what work is, so that what's left over can be rest.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat according to halacha study the categories of work and their derivatives, and rabbis apply them to new situations; other Jews keep Shabbat through rest, meals and synagogue in their own ways.

an act can count as work even if it isn't on the list by name

games.q: you're a student in the study house. the tabernacle needed dyes cooked, but the Mishnah's list says baking. what do you do?
o: ask why, and look for a pattern in the list.
games.why: the Talmud asks exactly this, and answers that the Mishnah followed the order of bread. the list is built in chains, field to loaf.

practice: Pick something you did yesterday with your hands or a screen, cooking, typing, fixing, carrying, and play the rabbis' game with it.
Is it making something new, changing a thing from one state to another, or moving it from place to place? Find its father, and simply see it as a kind of making; you don't have to stop doing it.
